title: Sou português, estou cansado — two verbs for "to be"
goal: Choose between *ser* and *estar* without long deliberation — the second hurdle, and the one place in this course where the wrong choice really **changes the meaning** of your sentence instead of just making it sound odd.
bekal: say the six forms of *estar* as smoothly as *ser*
know when an adjective takes *ser* and when it takes *estar*
ask *Como estás?* and answer it honestly

dialogs.title: Diálogo — À porta do café
dialogs.intro: Three days later, Budi runs into Ana again outside a small café in Bairro Alto.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Estou cansado. O quarto é bom, mas a cama é dura.
lines.id: I'm tired. The room is nice, but the bed is hard.
lines.literal: I-am(estar) tired(m). the room is(ser) good, but the bed is(ser) hard.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: Poor you! And today, are you free?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Estou. Estou de férias até segunda-feira.
lines.id: I am. I'm on vacation until Monday.
lines.literal: I-am. I-am of vacation until second-day.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Boa! O café aqui é ótimo... mas hoje está fechado.
lines.id: Great! The coffee here is excellent... but today it's closed.
lines.literal: good(f)! the café here is(ser) excellent... but today it-is(estar) closed.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What a pity! Are you in a hurry?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Não, estou tranquila. Sou estudante, e hoje não há aulas.
lines.id: No, I'm in no rush. I'm a student, and there are no classes today.
lines.literal: no, I-am(estar) calm(f). I-am(ser) student, and today not there-is classes.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: De história. E tu? És estudante também?
lines.id: History. And you? Are you a student too?
lines.literal: of history. and you? you-are student also?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Não, sou engenheiro. Estou aqui para aprender português.
lines.id: No, I'm an engineer. I'm here to learn Portuguese.
lines.literal: no, I-am(ser) engineer. I-am(estar) here for to-learn Portuguese.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: O português é difícil, mas tu estás a falar muito bem!
lines.id: Portuguese is hard, but you're speaking really well!
lines.literal: the Portuguese is difficult, but you you-are at to-speak very well!

notes: **Como estás? not Como és?** Both are correct sentences, but they mean very different things. *Como estás?* = "how are you?" — asking about your state today. *Como és?* = "what are you like?" — asking about your character. Mixing them up with someone you've just met produces a far more personal question than you intended.

**O café é ótimo, mas está fechado.** One sentence, two verbs, and the whole difference is right there. The café **is** a great place — that's a lasting quality, so *ser*. It **is** closed today — that's a temporary state, so *estar*. If you remember only one example from this unit, remember this one.

**Sou engenheiro, without um.** Portuguese **uses no article** before professions: *Sou engenheiro*, *É professora*, *Somos estudantes*. Adding *um* (*sou um engenheiro*) sounds as if you're making a point — "I'll have you know I'm an engineer". English does the opposite ("I'm *an* engineer"), so be careful not to translate word for word in your head.

**Não há aulas** — *há* means "there is / there are", for things and situations, singular or plural. It has only one form and never changes: *há um problema* (there's a problem), *há muitos livros* (there are many books). It comes from the verb *haver*, which at A1 practically only appears in this form.

**Estás a falar** — the typically Portuguese "-ing" form: *estar a* + infinitive. In Brazil people say *está falando*. This form is fully covered in Unit 13; for now, just recognize it when it appears.
**Coitado / coitada** agrees with the person being pitied, just like *obrigado* agrees with the speaker. Ana says *coitado* because Budi is the tired one.

grammars.title: Estar — the verb for "being" somewhere or in some state
body: Its forms are irregular but follow an easy pattern: they all start with *est-*, and the *e* at the front almost disappears when spoken.
after: In fast speech the Portuguese often chop off the first syllable entirely: *tou bem* for *estou bem*, *tás pronto?* for *estás pronto?*. Don't copy it yet, but do recognize it — otherwise you'll hear something that isn't in any dictionary.
Notice that *estar* and *ser* both use one form for *vocês*, *eles* and *elas* — and in both it ends in *-ão*: *são*, *estão*.

grammars.title: Ser or estar? One question settles nine cases out of ten
body: Ask yourself: **will this still be true next month?** If yes, use *ser*. If not, use *estar*.

head: To express
Verb
Examples
rows: *A Ana é simpática. O livro é interessante.*
*A chave está na mesa. Estou em Lisboa.*
*A loja está fechada. O café está frio.*

after: **One exception to memorize:** the location of buildings and cities, which can't move, may take *ser* or *ficar*: *Lisboa é em Portugal* or *Lisboa fica em Portugal*. For things that can be moved, always *estar*: *O livro está na mesa*.

**And one English trap:** "I am hungry" is translated with *ter*, not *ser* or *estar* — *tenho fome*, literally "I have hunger". Likewise *tenho sede* (I'm thirsty), *tenho frio* (I'm cold), *tenho sono* (I'm sleepy), *tenho medo* (I'm scared). The verb *ter* is covered in Unit 5.

grammars.title: Adjectives that change meaning with the verb
body: A group of adjectives can be used with both — and the meaning really changes. This is proof that choosing *ser* or *estar* isn't just grammatical tidiness.

head: Adjective
With **ser**
With **estar**
rows: *está rico* — flush with cash at the moment

after: That last pair is the most useful to remember. *A Ana é bonita* compliments her looks; *A Ana está bonita hoje* compliments how she looks today — and the second is actually what the Portuguese say more often, because it sounds lighter and less like a judgment.

blocks.text: All the adjectives below are used with **estar**, and they all change with the speaker's gender. Men use the *-o* form, women the *-a* form.

The last two use a preposition, not an adjective: *estar com* (with) and *estar de* (in a state of). The *estar de* pattern is very productive in Portugal: *estou de folga* (I'm off work), *estou de acordo* (I agree), *estou de pé* (I'm standing).

blocks.title: Three ways to answer "Como estás?"
items: **Neutral:** *Estou bem, obrigado. E tu?* — always safe.
**Very Portuguese:** *Vai-se andando.* ("getting by") or *Mais ou menos.* ("so-so") — both honest and heard all the time.
**Keep it short.** Just like English "how are you?", this is mostly small talk. If things really are bad, the Portuguese flag it first with *Ai...* or *Olha...* before telling the story.

blocks.text: Notice two words that **don't change** for gender: *estudante* and *motorista*. Only the article tells them apart — *o estudante* and *a estudante*. Every word ending in *-ista* behaves this way: *o/a dentista*, *o/a jornalista*, *o/a artista*.

To ask about someone's job, two questions are both natural: *O que é que fazes?* ("what do you do?") and *Qual é a tua profissão?* ("what's your profession?"). The first is far more common in everyday conversation — and notice the *o que é que* construction, which you'll meet again and again in Unit 4.

items: How are you? I'm fine, thanks.
The café is nice, but today it's closed.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
Spaced review — unit 1. Translate into Portuguese without looking back at the unit.

answers: sou — estou — está — é — está — estamos
Como estás? Estou bem, obrigado. — Sou professor. — O café é bom, mas hoje está fechado. — Ela está ocupada. — A chave está na mesa. — Hoje não há aulas.
Como estás? — Hoje estou cansada. — Não sou engenheiro. — O café está fechado. — Hoje estamos livres.
Boa tarde! Tudo bem? — Chamo-me Budi. — Muito prazer. — De onde és? — Até logo!
